newsitem.title: USA: U.S. public power group urges tax law change.
newsitem.headline: U.S. public power group urges tax law change.

text.p: Large U.S. public power systems urged senators Thursday to change a tax law that limits the ability of state or locally-owned power utilities to sell power or transmission capacity to private entities.
Under a 1986 tax law, state or municipal utilities are barred from selling more than 10 percent of their power or transmission capacity to other power sellers.
The so-called "private use" rule was designed to ensure that private power systems did not benefit unfairly from tax exemptions reserved for nonprofit units of state and local government.

The Large Public Power Council said the rule was now handicapping them, blocking them from selling their power through investor-owned utilities' transmission lines, which are now required to be open to all power producers.

"Public power cannot comply with federal energy policy and federal tax policy at the same time," said Missy Mandell, an executive director for the Lower Colorado River Authority, a member of the Large Public Power Council.
"We must resolve this IRS (Internal Revenue Service) restriction," she said at a Senate Energy Committee workshop on public power and electricity deregulation.
Mandell said a public power system could lose tax-exempt status on its bonds if it wanted to compete against other power providers by breaking the private use rule.
But if state and local power systems failed to compete, they could lose customers to other power providers.

"State or local systems face a Hobson's choice -- either violate the private use rules and cause their debt to become taxable, penalizing hundreds of thousands of bondholders, or leave that capacity idle ... and saddle its remaining customer-owners with the debt for the facility," she said.

Because of the private use rule, public power groups also may not be able to take part in new arrangements linking utility transmission lines under independent system operators, which federal regulators have encouraged.

The workshop on the role of public power in a deregulated electricity market highlighted public power's opposition to a federal mandate on states to open their markets to competition, which would cut into public power monopolies.
Public power systems supply 25 percent of all electricity in the United States.
Investor-owned utilities have said lawmakers must take away subsidies to public power if the federal government requires states to deregulate power sales.

In electricity deregulation bills introduced so far, only investor-owned utilities would be required to open their distribution lines to other power providers, with lawmakers loath to touch public power.
